Circular flow is a simple model showing how HOUSEHOLDS and FIRMS interact in two linked markets: the factor market (inputs) and the product market (goods and services).

1. Real flow: households supply factors of production (labor, land, capital, entrepreneurship) to firms, and firms produce goods and services that go back to households through the product market.
2. Monetary flow: firms pay households wages, rent, interest, and profit for those factors, and households use that income to buy the goods and services firms sell (firms receive revenue).

In the basic version of the model, the key assumptions are: no government, no international trade, no financial markets, and all household income is spent on consumption. That implies the simple spending identity

$$
Y = C
$$

and the accounting idea

$$
Y = \text{Income} = \text{Expenditure}
$$

2) Nominal GDP (each year)
Use that year’s prices and that year’s quantities:

$$Y_t = P_{F,t}Q_{F,t} + P_{C,t}Q_{C,t}$$

Here $F$ is food, $C$ is clothes, and $t$ is the year (2023, 2024, 2025).

3) Real GDP (pick a base year first)
With base year $b$, hold prices fixed at base-year prices:

$$y_t^{(b)} = P_{F,b}Q_{F,t} + P_{C,b}Q_{C,t}$$

4) GDP deflator (consistent with your base year)
Compute nominal and real for the SAME year $t$ (and same base year for real), then:

$$\text{Deflator}_t = \frac{Y_t}{y_t^{(b)}}\times 100$$

5) CPI (fixed basket method; pick a base year first)
Define the “basket” as the base-year quantities $(Q_{F,b}, Q_{C,b})$. Cost that same basket at each year’s prices:

$$\text{BasketCost}_t = P_{F,t}Q_{F,b} + P_{C,t}Q_{C,b}$$

Then index it:

$$\text{CPI}_t = \frac{\text{BasketCost}_t}{\text{BasketCost}_b}\times 100$$

6) Economic growth
“Economic growth” means output rises in REAL terms, so you’ll want to look at real GDP growth (and not nominal, which mixes in price changes).

Porter’s framework is a way to predict average INDUSTRY profitability by checking the competitive pressures around firms:

$$
\text{Industry Profitability} = f(\text{Buyer power},\ \text{Supplier power},\ \text{Rivalry},\ \text{Threat of Entry},\ \text{Substitutes},\ \text{Complements})
$$

1. Bargaining power of buyers: buyers can force prices down or demand more value if they have good alternatives, low switching costs, or large volume.
2. Bargaining power of suppliers: suppliers can raise input prices or restrict quality/terms if they’re concentrated or hard to replace.
3. Rivalry among competitors: firms compete away profits via price cuts, advertising, faster product cycles, etc., especially when products are similar and growth is slow.
4. Threat of new entrants: if entry is easy (low fixed costs, weak scale/network effects, easy access to distribution), incumbents can’t sustain high margins.
5. Substitutes: different products that satisfy the same need cap willingness-to-pay (they put a ceiling on price).
6. Complements: products that increase willingness-to-pay for yours (if complements get cheaper/better, demand for your product can rise; if complements worsen, demand can fall).

In your slides, “Government/Regulation” and “Technology” sit outside because they can SHIFT any of the six forces (for example, by changing entry costs, switching costs, or which rivals you face).

prior_turns.content: when to use babe's rule and when to use conditional probability formula

You’re deciding between:

$$\Pr(A|B)=\frac{\Pr(A\cap B)}{\Pr(B)}$$

versus Bayes’ rule

$$\Pr(A|B)=\frac{\Pr(B|A)\Pr(A)}{\Pr(B)}$$

Same object on the left, different inputs on the right. The conditional probability definition is most direct when you ALREADY have the joint probability $\Pr(A\cap B)$ (or can get it easily) and the marginal $\Pr(B)$. Bayes’ rule is the rewrite you use when you DON’T have $\Pr(A\cap B)$, but you DO have the “reverse” conditional $\Pr(B|A)$ plus $\Pr(A)$ (and you can get $\Pr(B)$).

Concrete check: in your problem, do you have $\Pr(A\cap B)$ available, or do you instead have something like $\Pr(B|A)$ and $\Pr(A)$ (the “given” is flipped)?
